extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and legal practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: A cross-jurisdictional overview of defamation (libel and slander) explaining definitions, the elements required for a claim, common defences, remedies, and notable variations between legal systems and international human-rights guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation is a communication that injures a third party's reputation and causes a legally redressable injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The precise legal definition varies by country; defamation is not necessarily restricted to making assertions that are false and can extend to concepts such as dignity and honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel versus slander (form distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the English-speaking world, the law traditionally distinguishes between libel (written, printed, posted online, published in mass media) and slander (oral speech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fundamental distinction lies in the form of publication; fleeting forms (spoken words, gestures) are slander while written/printed/pictures or other non-spoken forms are libel. Some statutes treat broadcast speech as libel rather than slander.

rubrics_metrics.name: General elements of a defamation claim (common law)
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute defamation, a claim must generally be false and must have been made to someone other than the person defamed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many common-law jurisdictions require falsity and publication to a third party; additional jurisdiction-specific elements (e.g., fault, damages) may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical American four-part requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff typically must prove that the defendant: (1) made a false and defamatory statement concerning the plaintiff; (2) shared the statement with a third party; (3) if the defamatory matter is of public concern, acted at least negligently; and (4) caused damages to the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For public officials or other legitimate public figures, American courts require proof of 'actual malice' (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of fact versus opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a false statement of fact (as opposed to opinion) can be defamatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements of opinion are inherently non-falsifiable and generally protected; however, statements labeled as opinion can be actionable if they imply provably false facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth / justification defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving the truth of an allegedly defamatory statement is always a valid defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions apply doctrines like 'substantial truth' (slight inaccuracies won’t defeat the defence if the gist is true) or statutory provisions allowing partial-truth defences when unproven charges do not materially injure reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest / responsible communication defence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to show there is a well-founded public interest in the specific information being widely known, which may operate as a defence even for public figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public interest is generally 'what is in the interest of the public', not merely what interests the public. Responsible journalism and accurate reporting may inform the availability of the defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege (absolute and qualified)
rubrics_metrics.description: Privilege is a circumstance that justifies or excuses an act that would otherwise constitute a tort; absolute privilege bars suits even if statements are made maliciously, while qualified privilege is a more limited protection (e.g., journalists in some circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical examples of absolute privilege include evidence given in court and statements made in legislative sessions (parliamentary privilege). Qualified privilege may apply to public meetings, local government documents, and communications made in the public interest, subject to conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake of fact (good-faith belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made in a good faith and reasonable belief that they were true are generally treated the same as true statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may inquire into the reasonableness of the belief; the expected degree of care varies with the defendant (e.g., a newspaper is expected to check multiple sources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere vulgar abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: An insult that is not intended to be taken literally or believed, or likely to cause real damage to a reputation, is not necessarily defamatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vituperative statements made in anger (e.g., calling someone an abusive name during an argument) are often considered non-actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made with an honest belief in their soundness on a matter of public interest (such as regarding official acts) are defendable against a defamation claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fair comment is protected even if the argument is logically unsound; protection exists if a reasonable person could honestly entertain such an opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent defence
rubrics_metrics.description: In rare cases, a defendant can argue that the plaintiff consented to the dissemination of the statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent negates the wrongful publication element but will be rare and fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innocent dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant is not liable if they had no actual knowledge of the defamatory statement or no reason to believe the statement was defamatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defence can protect intermediaries (e.g., delivery services) but can be defeated if the lack of knowledge was due to negligence or the intermediary had notice and acted negligently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incapability of further defamation / 'libel-proof' plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, it was a defence that the claimant's position in the community is so poor that defamation could not do further damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where applicable, a plaintiff whose reputation is already so diminished may be unable to prove further injury; modern application varies by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jurisdictions require that a lawsuit be brought within a limited period of time; for mass media publication the limitation period begins at the time of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness rules vary across jurisdictions and media; plaintiffs who delay may be barred by statutes of limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No third-party communication (publication requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If no one other than the plaintiff and defendant heard the false statement, there is no defamation recourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication to at least one third party is typically a required element of a defamation claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: No actual injury requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a third party hearing the defamatory statement does not believe the statement, or does not care, then there is no injury and therefore no recourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions require proof of actual damage except in defamation-per-se categories where injury is presumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation per se categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Some false statements are so damaging that they create a presumption of injury; common categories include: accusing someone of a crime, alleging a foul or loathsome disease, adversely reflecting on a person's fitness to conduct business or trade, and imputing serious sexual misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In per se cases a plaintiff need not prove special damages to proceed to verdict, though proving actual damages may be necessary for full compensation; truth remains an absolute defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies available to successful plaintiffs vary and range from damages to court orders requiring the defendant to retract the offending statement or to publish a correction or an apology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions also allow punitive damages or injunctions; courts may require proof of serious harm for certain plaintiffs (e.g., corporations in some jurisdictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate defamation rules vary
rubrics_metrics.description: Common law jurisdictions vary on whether they permit corporate plaintiffs; examples: Australia generally denies private corporations the right to sue (with small-business exceptions), Canada grants corporations similar rights as individuals, and England requires private corporations to prove serious harm and serious financial loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory reform in some places tailors the ability of corporations to sue and the required showing of harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public figure / actual malice (U.S. rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: For public officials (and other legitimate public figures) to win a libel case in an American court, the statement must have been published knowing it to be false or with reckless disregard for the truth (actual malice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This heightened fault standard stems from New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964) and limits liability for media/public debate on matters of public concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial truth doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The American doctrine of substantial truth provides that a statement is not defamatory if it has 'slight inaccuracies of expression' but is otherwise true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor imprecisions will not render an otherwise true statement actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-SLAPP / procedural special motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tort-reform measures (anti-SLAPP laws) enable defendants to make a special motion to strike or dismiss during which discovery is suspended and which, if successful, would terminate the lawsuit and allow the party to recover its legal costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural devices are intended to protect public participation and make vexatious defamation suits less effective as tools of censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actio iniuriarum (Roman Dutch and Scots law elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability under the actio iniuriarum involves elements such as harm (violation of personality interests: corpus, dignitas and fama), wrongful conduct, and intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In these systems harm is the infringement of a personality right; Scots law commonly recognizes veritas (proving the truth) as a defence. Intention (animus iniuriandi) may be required for some remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-rights balancing test for restrictions (three-part test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations must be: 1) 'provided by law that is clear and accessible to everyone', 2) 'proven to be necessary and legitimate to protect the rights or reputations of others', and 3) 'proportionate and the least restrictive to achieve the purported aim'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This three-part test (from the UN Human Rights Committee) is analogous to other proportionality tests (e.g., Oakes Test) and is used to assess whether domestic defamation law appropriately balances reputation protection and freedom of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: UN Human Rights Committee General comment No. 34 guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation laws must be crafted with care so they do not serve to stifle freedom of expression; laws should include defences such as the defence of truth and should not be applied to forms of expression not subject to verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee suggests avoiding penalizing untrue statements published in error without malice about public figures, recognizing public interest as a defence, avoiding excessively punitive measures, considering decriminalization of defamation, and that imprisonment is never an appropriate penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal defamation (existence and cautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to tort law, many jurisdictions treat defamation as a criminal offence and provide for penalties as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International bodies urge caution: criminal defamation laws are increasingly used to censor critics; where criminalization exists it should be limited to the most serious cases and avoid imprisonment; Article 19 and NGOs map criminal-defamation laws globally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media liability insurance considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Media liability or defamation insurance is often purchased by publishers and journalists to cover potential damage awards from libel lawsuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insurers may advise worldwide coverage to defend against suits filed in favourable jurisdictions; investigative journalism often requires higher premiums and may be excluded from some policies. Much of insurer payments go to legal costs rather than settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional variation and related causes of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws vary by jurisdiction; related torts or delicts (e.g., negligent misrepresentation, false light, invasion of privacy, harassment) may overlap with or provide alternative remedies distinct from defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences arise from case law, statutes, and constitutional concerns; practitioners must consider local doctrines, statutory reforms, and unique remedies (e.g., false-light in the U.S., misrepresentation, trademark dilution).
